Polynomial Bohnenblust–Hille Bounds
for product of cyclic groups
A Potts-hypercontractive weighted bootstrap

Joseph Slote    Alexander Volberg
September 3, 2026
Abstract

Fix an integer K≥2K\geq 2, and let CKn={(e2​π​i​jK)j=0K−1}nC_{K}^{n}=\{(e^{\frac{2\pi ij}{K}})_{j=0}^{K-1}\}^{n} be the product of cyclic groups of order KK. For a Fourier character χα\chi_{\alpha}, let s⁡(α)s(\alpha) be the number of active coordinates. We give a self-contained proposed proof that the dimension-free Bohnenblust–Hille constants governed by interaction order grow polynomially: if pd=2​d/(d+1)p_{d}=2d/(d+1) and

γ2=12,γK=K​log⁡(K−1)4​(K−2)(K≥3),\gamma_{2}=\frac{1}{2},\qquad\gamma_{K}=\frac{K\log(K-1)}{4(K-2)}\quad(K\geq 3),

then the ℓpd\ell^{p_{d}} norm of Fourier coefficients {f^​(α)}\{\hat{f}(\alpha)\} is bounded by L∞L^{\infty} norm of ff multiplied by C⁡(K)​d4​γK+5C(K)d^{4\gamma_{K}+5}. The constant C⁡(K)C(K) is actually at most of the order K5/2K^{5/2}.

1 Introduction

We were made aware of the paper [12] on September 7. It was published online on August 27. For Hamming cube case K=2K=2 it has the same result with a slightly worse exponent.

Bohnenblust–Hille inequality has an old and venerable history. It was first proved in [3] in 1931 and gave the nn-free estimate of a certain coefficient norm of an analytic polynomial of variables nn via its maximum on multi-torus 𝕋n\mathbb{T}^{n}. The constant was independent of nn but dependent in a superexponential fashion on the degree mm of the polynomial. The result was needed to answer a question of Harold Bohr concerning a convergence property of Dirichlet series.

Much later this result was revised and the constant was improved in [6], and the constant became exponential in degreee mm.

A bit later [1] proved a subexponential in mm estimate for multi-torus case.

Very soon [7] proved a similar subexponential estimate for polynomials on Hamming cube.

This latter result was used in a learning theory by Eskenazis–Ivanisvili [9] to obtain an optimal number of queries to PAC (probably approximately correct) learning of function of low degree on Boolean cube.

In note [24] we gave a polynomial in degree estimate for the constant of the Bohnenblast–Hille inequality on Boolean cube.

The argument in [24] adapted the weighted graded square-function method introduced in Pellegrino and Teixeira [19] Section 5. There it was introduced for analytic polynomials. There are several new and exciting ideas in [19]. One of them is a bicoloring of variables, another is a special square function on coefficients of polynomials.

On the Boolean cube, Bonami–Beckner hypercontractivity supplies simultaneous row and column control after a random bicoloring of the coordinates. Bicoloring idea comes from [19], but in the case of Hamming cube it can be realized in a simpler way. Every monomial on Hamming cube is square-free, so the dominant-power compression regime from the analytic setting disappears.

The current note is devoted to Bohnenblust–Hille inequality on cyclic group. Now we have K≥3K\geq 3 and the group CKC_{K} of KK-th roots of unity. Polynomial FF of nn variables on CKnC_{K}^{n} has total degree mm but the degree in each variable is at most K−1K-1.

Such nn-free Bohnenblust–Hille inequality was proved in [2], [21], but the constant was exponential in the degree mm of the polynomial (and of course also depending on KK).

Here the polynomial in mm estimate is obtained. The method repeats this of [19] Section 5 by exploring the excited ideas introduced in this paper.

Also the proof follows closely the one in [24], but with some caveats. For example, in the cyclic group situation we know [21], [5] that the spectral projection on the linear combination of monomials zαz^{\alpha} such that the cardinality of supp⁡α\operatorname{supp}\alpha has an estimate independent on dimension nn.

On Hamming cube (K=2K=2) such spectral projection is the same as the projection on the fixed homogeneity part, but for K≥3K\geq 3 these are two different things.

Bohnenblust–Hille inequality on cyclic groups was used to get a quantum Bohnenblust–Hille inequality [22], [21], Interestingly the constant is exponential in mm because of the reduction of non-commutative case to the commutative cyclic group case. But what is even more interesting is that this exponential nature of the non-commutative Bohnenblust–Hille inequality cannot be made sub-exponential, see [20].

The architecture of the proof repeats this of [19] Section 5 to a large extent. It is the weighted graded bootstrap of Pellegrino–Teixeira: a weighted square function, simultaneous row and column control, and a strict binary-entropy contraction for balanced two-block degrees.

Its implementation on support layers follows the Boolean-cube argument [24]: whole-coordinate random bicoloring, exact reconstruction of the parent Fourier index, binomial central capture, and a separate low-level estimate.

The support mode splitting is much more suitable here than the homogeneous degree mode splitting. This phenomena was already noticed in [21] and in [5], but [5], gives a much better estimate on the spectral projection L∞L^{\infty} norm that the one in [21]. This better estimate is crucial, it is used in Lemma 3.5 below.

The only new high-degree analytic input taken from the cyclic-group paper of Pellegrino–Raposo Junior [18] is its Potts hypercontractive radius ρ≤(p−1)γK\rho\leq(p-1)^{\gamma_{K}}. Three fixed low interaction levels are closed using the previously known support-sensitive cyclic Bohnenblust–Hille inequality and an interior Bernstein estimate. An explicit contraction constant 0.8207730.820773 important for bootstrapping argument that finishes the proof. It is obtained uniformly in KK.

1.1 The problem and the proposed result

Let

CK={1,ω,…,ωK−1},ω=e2​π​i/K,C_{K}=\{1,\omega,\ldots,\omega^{K-1}\},\qquad\omega=\mathrm{e}^{2\pi i/K},

with normalized counting measure. We identify CKC_{K} with ℤ/K​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/K\mathbb{Z} and work multiplicatively because this makes the Fourier characters monomials. For α∈{0,…,K−1}N\alpha\in\{0,\ldots,K-1\}^{N}, set

χα​(x)=xα=∏j=1Nxjαj,s⁡(α)=#⁡{j:αj≠0}.\chi_{\alpha}(x)=x^{\alpha}=\prod_{j=1}^{N}x_{j}^{\alpha_{j}},\qquad s(\alpha)=\#\{j:\alpha_{j}\neq 0\}.

The quantity s⁡(α)s(\alpha) is the interaction order. It records the number of coordinates on which the character depends, independently of the local nonzero degrees αj∈{1,…,K−1}\alpha_{j}\in\{1,\ldots,K-1\}.

Pellegrino and Raposo Junior recently proved a subexponential bound for the corresponding dimension-free constants and, in particular, for the larger interaction-order class [18]. The purpose of this note is to show that the weighted entropy mechanism of Pellegrino and Teixeira [19], when combined with Potts hypercontractivity, appears to improve the degree dependence from subexponential to polynomial.

Our main statement is the following.

Theorem 1.1 (Proposed polynomial cyclic Bohnenblust–Hille bound).

For every fixed integer K≥2K\geq 2, there is a constant CK<∞C_{K}<\infty such that, for every d,N≥1d,N\geq 1 and every complex-valued function f:CKN→ℂf:C_{K}^{N}\to\mathbb{C} whose Fourier transform is supported on s⁡(α)≤ds(\alpha)\leq d,

(∑s⁡(α)≤d|f^​(α)|pd)1/pd≤CK​d4​γK+5​‖f‖∞,pd=2​dd+1.\left(\sum_{s(\alpha)\leq d}\left\lvert\widehat{f}(\alpha)\right\rvert^{p_{d}}\right)^{1/p_{d}}\leq C_{K}d^{4\gamma_{K}+5}\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\infty},\qquad p_{d}=\frac{2d}{d+1}. (1)

Here

γ2=12,γK=K​log⁡(K−1)4​(K−2)(K≥3).\gamma_{2}=\frac{1}{2},\qquad\gamma_{K}=\frac{K\log(K-1)}{4(K-2)}\quad(K\geq 3). (2)

Consequently, for K≥3K\geq 3 the displayed power is

4​γK+5=5+K​log⁡(K−1)K−2.4\gamma_{K}+5=5+\frac{K\log(K-1)}{K-2}. (3)

The same bound holds for functions of canonical total degree at most dd.

The result is for fixed KK. The multiplicative constant may depend on KK, and the exponent itself grows like 5+log⁡K5+\log K as K→∞K\to\infty. The constant γK\gamma_{K} is exactly half the reciprocal of the classical complete-graph of KK vertices log-Sobolev constant, see [8].

1.2 Provenance of the ingredients

Because the proof combines several recent ideas, it is useful to separate precisely what comes from where.

The Pellegrino–Teixeira architecture.

The following high-level devices are taken from the weighted stage of [19]:

  • •

    the weighted graded square function and its bootstrap constant;

  • •

    simultaneous row and column estimates for all bidegrees;

  • •

    the fractional two-block coefficient interpolation;

  • •

    the variable-angle mixed summation lemma;

  • •

    the conversion of balanced bidegrees into a strict binary-entropy contraction, followed by bootstrapping argument

The Pellegrino–Teixeira paper also supplies the general ancestry philosophy: a two-block descendant must retain enough information to recover its parent coefficient before absolute values are taken. Its actual analytic splitting scheme is not copied verbatim here. All estimates needed in the present support-layer implementation are reproduced below. We do not use the Pellegrino–Teixeira dominant-power compression, an active coordinate contributes one support unit, regardless of its local frequency degree.

The Boolean-cube adaptation.

The passage from analytic homogeneous degree to support layers grading follows the Boolean companion argument rather than the literal analytic split:

  • •

    random bicoloring is performed on whole active coordinates, not on units of algebraic exponent;

  • •

    the pair of colored restrictions retains every local degree and uniquely recovers the parent Fourier index;

  • •

    the number of active coordinates sent to either block is binomial, which gives a uniform central-capture probability;

  • •

    a finite ambient-dimension cutoff is introduced before bootstrapping, so finiteness is not assumed circularly;

  • •

    the few low support levels are extracted by a one-variable noise polynomial and an interior Bernstein estimate.

The cyclic case has an asymmetric negative-noise interval, but this interval still contains zero in its interior. This is the only modification needed in the low-level projection argument.

The cyclic-group paper.

The only genuinely new high-degree analytic input imported from Pellegrino–Raposo Junior [18] is Potts hypercontractivity [8], [10]:

‖Tρ⊗N​g‖2≤‖g‖pfor0≤ρ≤(p−1)γK.\left\lVert T_{\rho}^{\otimes N}g\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{p}\quad\text{for}\quad 0\leq\rho\leq(p-1)^{\gamma_{K}}.

Their interaction-order notation and Fourier normalization are also adopted. The present proof does not use their homogenization, symmetric multilinear form, orbit normalization, mixed polarization, block recurrence, or asymptotic optimization.

Known information on L2→LpL^{2}\to L^{p} hypercontractivity of the specific noise operator on cyclic group CKC_{K}.

There are several different noise operators on functions on CKnC_{K}^{n}. One is Tρ⊗nT_{\rho}^{\otimes n}, where

Tρ​χj=ρψ⁡(j)​χj,ψ⁡(j)=min⁡(j,K−j).T_{\rho}\chi_{j}=\rho^{\psi(j)}\chi_{j},\quad\psi(j)=\min(j,K-j)\,.

another one is Tρ⊗nT_{\rho}^{\otimes n} with just

Tρ=ρ​I+(1−ρ)​𝔼.T_{\rho}=\rho I+(1-\rho)\mathbb{E}\,.

The latter one is responsible for the so-called Potts hypercontractivity and its hypercontractive properties are studied in [8], [10]. It is known that (2,p)(2,p) hypercontractivity happens with

ρ=(p−1)γK.\rho=(p-1)^{\gamma_{K}}.

Even though we do not need the first one we list below some known results with ρ\rho that gives hypercontractivity.

The short historical answer is:

For K=3K=3, the sharp value is different and comes from the Latała-Oleszkiewicz biased two-point inequality via Wolff’s reduction.

K=4K=4: Beckner-Janson-Jerison (1983), (p−1)1/2(p-1)^{1/2} sharp, same as Boolean.

K=3K=3: Wolff + Latała-Oleszkiewicz, sharp L2→LpL^{2}\to L^{p}, different constant.

General KK: Junge-Palazuelos-Parcet-Perrin (2017), many optimal Lq→L2L^{q}\to L^{2} results for even qq.

2025–2026 preprints (Yao; Xie–Zhang): claim the Lq→LpL^{q}\to L^{p} full sharp constant ρ=p−1q−1,K≥4\rho=\sqrt{\frac{p-1}{q-1}},K\geq 4.

This is actually much closer to the Boolean world than one would have expected twenty years ago.

A small additional base-case input.

There is one caveat to the phrase "using Potts hypercontractivity". To close the levels r=1,2,3r=1,2,3, we also use the already-known dimension-free support-order Bohnenblust–Hille inequality, only in those three fixed degrees. This can be supplied independently by the support-sensitive Hamming-scheme theorem of Defant–Galicer–Mansilla–Mastyło–Muro [5]. No asymptotic information about its constants is used. Thus Potts hypercontractivity is the only cyclic-specific input in the high-degree bootstrap.

1.3 Important points in the proof

Before presenting the proof, we record the points at which the argument is most vulnerable and how they are resolved.

  1. 1.

    Circular finiteness. The weighted constant is first defined with an ambient cutoff NN. It is finite by finite dimensionality. Only after bootstrapping do we obtain a bound independent of NN.

  2. 2.

    Hypercontractive radius ρ\rho. The exact radius used below is ρ=(p−1)γK\rho=(p-1)^{\gamma_{K}}, with γK\gamma_{K} as in (2); this is Proposition 3.1 of [18].

  3. 3.

    Complex-valued functions. The Potts semigroup is positive. Hence |Tρ​g|≤Tρ​|g|\left\lvert T_{\rho}g\right\rvert\leq T_{\rho}\left\lvert g\right\rvert, so the real hypercontractive estimate extends with the same constant to complex functions.

  4. 4.

    Failure at one-coordinate bidegrees. The radius associated with p1=1p_{1}=1 vanishes. We therefore begin the central bootstrap at total interaction order 44 and explicitly require both block orders to be at least 22.

  5. 5.

    Modular collisions. A local degree of one variable is never split arithmetically modulo KK. The entire labeled coordinate is sent to one block. The two restrictions have disjoint coordinate supports and their union recovers the original frequency vector, so distinct parent coefficients cannot merge.

  6. 6.

    Noncontractive interaction projections. The projections f↦frf\mapsto f_{r} need not be L∞L^{\infty} contractions. They are used only for r≤3r\leq 3, where the extended Potts kernel is Markov on [−1/(K−1),1][-1/(K-1),1] and an interior Bernstein estimate gives a polynomial cost OK​(Mr)O_{K}(M^{r}).

  7. 7.

    Loss of entropy through the Potts radius. Removing the Potts weights costs at most 32​γK3^{2\gamma_{K}}, uniformly in the bidegrees. The weight exponent BK=4​γK+2B_{K}=4\gamma_{K}+2 compensates for this loss.

  8. 8.

    Numerical constant that allows us to use bootstrapping. The resulting contraction is bounded by

    c∗=0.8207720540​…<1c_{*}=0.8207720540\ldots<1

    uniformly in KK. The exact logarithmic estimate is displayed in Section 8.

  9. 9.

    Interaction order versus total degree. The theorem is first proved for interaction order. The total-degree corollary uses the canonical Fourier representatives αj∈{0,…,K−1}\alpha_{j}\in\{0,\ldots,K-1\} and the elementary inequality s⁡(α)≤∑jαjs(\alpha)\leq\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}.

2 Fourier notation and the constants

For f:CKN→ℂf:C_{K}^{N}\to\mathbb{C}, write

f⁡(x)=∑α∈{0,…,K−1}Nf^​(α)​χα​(x),f^​(α)=𝔼x​f​(x)​χα​(x)¯.f(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,\ldots,K-1\}^{N}}\widehat{f}(\alpha)\chi_{\alpha}(x),\qquad\widehat{f}(\alpha)=\mathbb{E}_{x}f(x)\overline{\chi_{\alpha}(x)}. (4)

The characters form an orthonormal basis, so Parseval gives

‖f‖22=∑α|f^​(α)|2.\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{\alpha}\left\lvert\widehat{f}(\alpha)\right\rvert^{2}. (5)

Decompose ff into exact interaction layers:

f=∑r=0Nfr,fr=∑s⁡(α)=rf^​(α)​χα.f=\sum_{r=0}^{N}f_{r},\qquad f_{r}=\sum_{s(\alpha)=r}\widehat{f}(\alpha)\chi_{\alpha}. (6)

For r≥1r\geq 1, put

pr=2​rr+1,Ar​(f)=(∑s⁡(α)=r|f^​(α)|pr)1/pr.p_{r}=\frac{2r}{r+1},\qquad A_{r}(f)=\left(\sum_{s(\alpha)=r}\left\lvert\widehat{f}(\alpha)\right\rvert^{p_{r}}\right)^{1/p_{r}}. (7)

For d≥1d\geq 1, let BHd,Kint\mathrm{BH}^{\mathrm{int}}_{d,K} be the least dimension-free constant such that

(∑s⁡(α)≤d|f^​(α)|pd)1/pd≤BHd,Kint​‖f‖∞\left(\sum_{s(\alpha)\leq d}\left\lvert\widehat{f}(\alpha)\right\rvert^{p_{d}}\right)^{1/p_{d}}\leq\mathrm{BH}^{\mathrm{int}}_{d,K}\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\infty} (8)

for all functions supported on interaction orders at most dd. Using the canonical representatives, define

|α|=α1+⋯+αN\left\lvert\alpha\right\rvert=\alpha_{1}+\cdots+\alpha_{N} (9)

and define BHd,Kdeg\mathrm{BH}^{\deg}_{d,K} analogously for Fourier support in |α|≤d\left\lvert\alpha\right\rvert\leq d. Since s⁡(α)≤|α|s(\alpha)\leq\left\lvert\alpha\right\rvert,

BHd,Kdeg≤BHd,Kint.\mathrm{BH}^{\deg}_{d,K}\leq\mathrm{BH}^{\mathrm{int}}_{d,K}. (10)

3 Analytic inputs

3.1 Potts hypercontractivity

For 0≤ρ≤10\leq\rho\leq 1, define

(Tρ​g)​(a)=ρ​g​(a)+(1−ρ)​𝔼​g,a∈CK.(T_{\rho}g)(a)=\rho g(a)+(1-\rho)\mathbb{E}g,\qquad a\in C_{K}. (11)

On the product, the coordinate operators commute and

Tρ⊗N​χα=ρs⁡(α)​χα.T_{\rho}^{\otimes N}\chi_{\alpha}=\rho^{s(\alpha)}\chi_{\alpha}. (12)
Theorem 3.1 (Potts hypercontractivity).

Let 1<p≤21<p\leq 2. For every N≥1N\geq 1 and every complex-valued g:CKN→ℂg:C_{K}^{N}\to\mathbb{C},

‖Tρ⊗N​g‖2≤‖g‖pwhenever0≤ρ≤(p−1)γK,\left\lVert T_{\rho}^{\otimes N}g\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{p}\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad 0\leq\rho\leq(p-1)^{\gamma_{K}}, (13)

where γK\gamma_{K} is given by (2). This is [18, Proposition 3.1].

For u≥2u\geq 2, the radius needed later is (with pu=2​uu+1p_{u}=\frac{2u}{u+1})

ρu=(pu−1)γK=(u−1u+1)γK.\rho_{u}=(p_{u}-1)^{\gamma_{K}}=\left(\frac{u-1}{u+1}\right)^{\gamma_{K}}. (14)

3.2 Fixed low interaction levels

The support-sensitive theorem of Defant–Galicer–Mansilla–Mastyło–Muro gives, for fixed KK, an exponential-in-rr dimension-free bound on interaction order at most rr [5, Theorem 2.13]. We use only r=1,2,3r=1,2,3.

Lemma 3.2 (Three fixed base levels).

For each fixed K≥2K\geq 2 and each r∈{1,2,3}r\in\{1,2,3\}, there is a constant βK,r<∞\beta_{K,r}<\infty, independent of NN, such that every exact interaction-rr function PP satisfies

Ar​(P)≤βK,r​‖P‖∞.A_{r}(P)\leq\beta_{K,r}\left\lVert P\right\rVert_{\infty}. (15)

3.3 An interior spectral-projection estimate

We use the elementary fact that the operator TρT_{\rho} of Potts hypercontractivity remains Markov on a certain real interval that contains 00 strictly inside.

Lemma 3.3 (The negative Potts interval).

For every

t∈IK:=[−1K−1,1],t\in I_{K}:=\left[-\frac{1}{K-1},1\right], (16)

the one-coordinate operator

Tt=Π+t⁡(I−Π),Π​g=(𝔼​g)​𝟏,T_{t}=\Pi+t(I-\Pi),\qquad\Pi g=(\mathbb{E}g)\mathbf{1},

is a Markov operator (averaging with transition probabilities). Consequently,

‖Tt⊗N​f‖∞≤‖f‖∞(t∈IK).\left\lVert T_{t}^{\otimes N}f\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\infty}\qquad(t\in I_{K}). (17)
Proof.

The transition kernel is

𝒦t(a,b)=t𝟏{a=b}+1−tK.\mathcal{K}_{t}(a,b)=t\mathbf{1}_{\{a=b\}}+\frac{1-t}{K}. (18)

Its diagonal entries are [1+(K−1)​t]/K[1+(K-1)t]/K, its off-diagonal entries are (1−t)/K(1-t)/K, and every row sums to one. These entries are nonnegative exactly for −1/(K−1)≤t≤1-1/(K-1)\leq t\leq 1. Tensor products preserve positivity and row sums. ∎

Remark 3.4.

The next lemma is very simple but very important. It suggests to split the polynomial on CKC_{K} not by the order of homogeneity, but by the order of the size of the support of monomials. This idea first appeared in [21], but the estimate of the spectral projections on such fixed support size peices of the polynomial was much worse than below. This idea is also used in [5].

Lemma 3.5 (Fixed-order interaction projection).

Fix K≥2K\geq 2 and an integer r≥1r\geq 1. There is a constant LK,r<∞L_{K,r}<\infty such that, whenever f:CKN→ℂf:C_{K}^{N}\to\mathbb{C} has interaction order at most MM,

‖fr‖∞≤LK,r​Mr​‖f‖∞.\left\lVert f_{r}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq L_{K,r}M^{r}\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\infty}. (19)
Proof.

Fix x∈CKNx\in C_{K}^{N} and form the one-variable polynomial

Px​(t)=Tt⊗N​f​(x)=∑j=0Mtj​fj​(x).P_{x}(t)=T_{t}^{\otimes N}f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{M}t^{j}f_{j}(x). (20)

By Lemma 3.3,

‖Px‖L∞​(IK)≤‖f‖∞.\left\lVert P_{x}\right\rVert_{L_{\infty}(I_{K})}\leq\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\infty}. (21)

Apply an affine change of variable from IKI_{K} to [−1,1][-1,1]. The point t=0t=0 is sent to

sK=−K−2K∈(−1,1).s_{K}=-\frac{K-2}{K}\in(-1,1).

If QxQ_{x} denotes the transformed polynomial and Gx​(θ)=Qx​(cos⁡θ)G_{x}(\theta)=Q_{x}(\cos\theta), then GxG_{x} is a trigonometric polynomial of degree at most MM. Bernstein’s inequality gives

‖Gx(j)‖∞≤Mj​‖Gx‖∞(j≥1).\left\lVert G_{x}^{(j)}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq M^{j}\left\lVert G_{x}\right\rVert_{\infty}\qquad(j\geq 1).

Since sKs_{K} is a fixed interior point for fixed KK, repeated differentiation of Qx​(s)=Gx​(arccos⁡s)Q_{x}(s)=G_{x}(\arccos s) at s=sKs=s_{K} gives

|Qx(r)​(sK)|≤CK,r​Mr​‖Qx‖L∞​[−1,1].\left\lvert Q_{x}^{(r)}(s_{K})\right\rvert\leq C_{K,r}M^{r}\left\lVert Q_{x}\right\rVert_{L_{\infty}[-1,1]}.

Undoing the affine change of variable and using Px(r)​(0)=r!​fr​(x)P_{x}^{(r)}(0)=r!f_{r}(x) proves (19). ∎

Corollary 3.6 (Low-level closure).

For every fixed K≥2K\geq 2 and every B>0B>0, there is a constant CK,B<∞C_{K,B}<\infty such that every ff of interaction order at most MM satisfies

[∑r=1min⁡{3,M}Ar​(f)2r2​B]1/2≤CK,B​M3​‖f‖∞.\left[\sum_{r=1}^{\min\{3,M\}}\frac{A_{r}(f)^{2}}{r^{2B}}\right]^{1/2}\leq C_{K,B}M^{3}\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\infty}. (22)

4 Mixed-norm tools

The next two lemmas are numerical. They do not depend on the underlying group.

Lemma 4.1 (Mixed-angle summation).

Let 0<a<1/20<a<1/2. Suppose ui,vi≥0u_{i},v_{i}\geq 0 satisfy ∑iui≤1\sum_{i}u_{i}\leq 1 and ∑ivi≤1\sum_{i}v_{i}\leq 1, and let θi∈[a,1−a]\theta_{i}\in[a,1-a]. Then

∑iuiθi​vi1−θi≤2​aa​(1−a)1−a=2​exp⁡{−h⁡(a)},\sum_{i}u_{i}^{\theta_{i}}v_{i}^{1-\theta_{i}}\leq 2a^{a}(1-a)^{1-a}=2\exp\{-h(a)\}, (23)

Proof.

Split the indices into I+={i:ui≥vi}I_{+}=\{i:u_{i}\geq v_{i}\} and I−={i:ui<vi}I_{-}=\{i:u_{i}<v_{i}\}. On I+I_{+}, uiθi​vi1−θi≤ui1−a​viau_{i}^{\theta_{i}}v_{i}^{1-\theta_{i}}\leq u_{i}^{1-a}v_{i}^{a}, while on I−I_{-}, uiθi​vi1−θi≤uia​vi1−au_{i}^{\theta_{i}}v_{i}^{1-\theta_{i}}\leq u_{i}^{a}v_{i}^{1-a}. Hölder’s inequality gives

∑iuiθi​vi1−θi≤U+1−a​V+a+U−a​V−1−a,\sum_{i}u_{i}^{\theta_{i}}v_{i}^{1-\theta_{i}}\leq U_{+}^{1-a}V_{+}^{a}+U_{-}^{a}V_{-}^{1-a},

where U±,V±U_{\pm},V_{\pm} are the corresponding partial masses. Enlarging unused mass, assume U++U−=V++V−=1U_{+}+U_{-}=V_{+}+V_{-}=1. Write U+=xU_{+}=x and V+=yV_{+}=y, with 0≤y≤x≤10\leq y\leq x\leq 1. A second application of Hölder yields

x1−a​ya+(1−x)a​(1−y)1−a≤(1+x−y)1−a​(1−x+y)a.x^{1-a}y^{a}+(1-x)^{a}(1-y)^{1-a}\leq(1+x-y)^{1-a}(1-x+y)^{a}.

With δ=x−y∈[0,1]\delta=x-y\in[0,1], the last expression is (1+δ)1−a​(1−δ)a(1+\delta)^{1-a}(1-\delta)^{a}. Its maximum occurs at δ=1−2​a\delta=1-2a and equals 2​aa​(1−a)1−a2a^{a}(1-a)^{1-a}. ∎

Lemma 4.2 (Two-block coefficient interpolation).

Let u,v≥1u,v\geq 1, set r=u+vr=u+v, and let c=(cα,β)c=(c_{\alpha,\beta}) be a finite scalar array. Then

5 The weighted row–column bootstrap

Fix B>0B>0 and integers M,N≥1M,N\geq 1. Define

𝒲B​(f)=[∑r=1MAr​(f)2r2​B]1/2\mathcal{W}_{B}(f)=\left[\sum_{r=1}^{M}\frac{A_{r}(f)^{2}}{r^{2B}}\right]^{1/2} (28)

ΓM,N(K)(B)=sup{𝒲B​(f)‖f‖∞:1≤n≤N,0≠f:CKn→ℂ,f^(α)=0 if s(α)>M}.\Gamma^{(K)}_{M,N}(B)=\sup\left\{\frac{\mathcal{W}_{B}(f)}{\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\infty}}:1\leq n\leq N,\quad 0\neq f:C_{K}^{n}\to\mathbb{C},\quad\widehat{f}(\alpha)=0\text{ if }s(\alpha)>M\right\}. (29)

For fixed M,NM,N, this is finite by finite dimensionality. The cutoff NN is retained until the contraction has been absorbed.

Remark 5.1.

The definition of 𝒲B​(F)\mathcal{W}_{B}(F) seems overcomplicated on the first glance. But in fact, its form has a simple explanation. This grading in homogeneity rr and keeping all r∈[1,M]r\in[1,M] together is enevitable by the following reason. As we cannot claim that Qω,d,eQ_{\omega,d,e} obtained from bounded FF has a nice L∞L^{\infty}  norm for fixed d,ed,e (see Addendum A for this claim), one is forced to consider the whole QωQ_{\omega} as the source of nice norm, but QωQ_{\omega} has of course many homogeneity modes; so one should invent a method to estimate all modes simultaneously—which explains the square function WB​(F)W_{B}(F) in formula (28) as a vehicle for subsequent estimates.

Remark 5.2.

We cannot exclude that by modifying the square function 𝒲B\mathcal{W}_{B} one can improve further the estimate.

Let IxI_{x} and IyI_{y} be the color classes. A character χα\chi_{\alpha} becomes

If s⁡(α)=rs(\alpha)=r, its xx-interaction order is the number of active coordinates colored xx, hence is distributed as Zr∼Bin⁡(r,1/2)Z_{r}\sim\Bin(r,1/2). Summing coefficient indicators proves (47).

π4=Pr{Z4=2}=38,\pi_{4}=\Pr\{Z_{4}=2\}=\frac{3}{8},

π5=Pr{Z5∈{2,3}}=58.\pi_{5}=\Pr\{Z_{5}\in\{2,3\}\}=\frac{5}{8}.

8 Uniform contraction and bootstrapping

Combining the preceding two sections gives a high-level contraction for any weight exponent BB.

Proposition 8.1 (High interaction levels).

For every B>0B>0 and every ff of interaction order at most MM,

[∑r=4MAr​(f)2r2​B]1/2≤cK,B​ΓM,N(K)​(B)​‖f‖∞,\left[\sum_{r=4}^{M}\frac{A_{r}(f)^{2}}{r^{2B}}\right]^{1/2}\leq c_{K,B}\Gamma^{(K)}_{M,N}(B)\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\infty}, (52)

where

cK,B=32​γK+5/8​51/8​2​exp⁡{−(B+12)​h​(14)}.c_{K,B}=3^{2\gamma_{K}+5/8}5^{1/8}\sqrt{2}\,\exp\left\{-\left(B+\frac{1}{2}\right)h\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\right\}. (53)

10 What is the difference with [18]

It is worth emphasizing the distinction between this argument and the subexponential recurrence of [18]. The latter proceeds by homogenizing a Fourier character into dd positions, passing to a symmetric dd-linear form, splitting the positions into blocks, and polarizing a mixed evaluation back to the diagonal. Its recurrence contains both a Potts loss and a binomial orbit–polarization loss.

None of those steps appears here. The weighted method works directly with the canonical Fourier coefficients and all interaction layers at once. A coordinate is colored as a whole, so the local degree of each variable is transported without alteration. The entropy gain from balanced support splits is paid once inside a square function and then absorbed. In that precise sense, the only part of the cyclic recurrence needed at high degree is its Potts hypercontractive estimate.

Remark 10.1 (Why modular arithmetic is harmless here).

The obstruction in cyclic polynomial extensions is often that products of local frequencies add modulo KK. The present splitting never multiplies or combines two frequencies on the same coordinate. It only records whether a coordinate-frequency pair belongs to the xx block or the yy block. Exact ancestry therefore survives unchanged.

Remark 10.2 (Why support order is the right parameter).

At the level of total algebraic degree, a character may contain a large local power xjK−1x_{j}^{K-1}. At the level of interaction order, that coordinate still contributes exactly one unit. Thus every interaction-order character is square-free in the geometry relevant to random coloring. This is the cyclic analogue of the absence of dominant powers on the Boolean cube.

Remark 10.3 (The Boolean endpoint).

For K=2K=2, γ2=1/2\gamma_{2}=1/2 and the argument gives the power d7d^{7}. This is the same weighted Boolean mechanism, with the central bootstrap started at level 44 rather than level 66 as it has been done in [24].

Remark 10.4 (Scope).

The estimate is polynomial in dd for each fixed KK. It is not uniform in KK: the exponent behaves as 5+log⁡K+o⁡(1)5+\log K+o(1), and the implicit constant also depends on KK through the three low-level estimates and the interior projection constants.
